pages.title: Week 1 Overview
pages.html:
🧑‍🔬 Redefining the Scientist – Beyond the Lab Coat

This week, we’re redefining what it means to be a scientist. You’ll use AI tools to visualize yourself as a real-world scientist, organize your notebook with a Variables Quick Reference, and make your first choice for the Science Fair project you’ll complete this quarter.

🤝 What to Expect This Week:

  • Read and review the Variables Quick Reference Guide

  • Create your AI Scientist image and reflection

  • Choose your Science Fair experiment (Checkpoint 1)

🎯 Spotlight Projects:

🤖 AI Scientist Creation Assignment

Use your imagination (and AI!) to show yourself as a real scientist in action.
You’ll design an experiment, identify variables, and bring your scientific story to life with creativity and accuracy.

Steps:

  1. Choose a science field that interests you (biology, chemistry, physics, marine science, etc.).

  2. Imagine a real experiment you could perform.

    • What will you change (independent variable)?

    • What will you measure (dependent variable)?

    • What must stay the same (controlled variables)?

  3. Use an AI image generator to create an image of yourself as that scientist performing your experiment.

  4. Write a short reflection (3–5 sentences):

    • Describe your experiment

    • Identify all 3 types of variables

    • Explain what your image shows about your role as a scientist

Submit:

  • Your AI image (download or screenshot)

  • Your reflection (typed in Canvas or written neatly and photographed)

🧩 Science Reference: Variables Quick Guide

Review this week’s Quick Reference Guide before creating your AI image.
It explains independent, dependent, and controlled variables and shows how scientists use them to design fair tests.

🔎 Mini Science Fair – Checkpoint 1

Review the list of possible Science Fair experiments.
Choose ONE that you’d like to complete this quarter.
Type your choice into the Canvas text box and submit.

💡 Reminder: You’ll have the entire quarter to complete your experiment and final video project. Some projects take time — DO NOT wait until the last second!

🧭 By the End of the Week, You’ll Be Able To:

✅ Explain what a scientist is — and what kind of scientist you could be
✅ Identify and apply all 3 types of variables in an experiment
✅ Visualize yourself as a scientist using creative AI tools
✅ Choose your first Science Fair experiment and commit to your project

📌 Remember:

🧠 Your AI creation shows scientific understanding — not just art
📚 Your Variables Quick Guide is a reference for the rest of the year
🚀 Checkpoint 1 is just the beginning — bigger projects are coming!
Scientists come in all forms — not just lab coats, but explorers, thinkers, and creators like you!

🌟 🧑‍🔬 Mission Briefing:

Redefine the scientist, visualize your experiment, and take your first step toward Science Fair success!

– Ms. Orlando 🌌🦈

pages.title: Week 2 Overview
pages.html:
🏙️ Elements in Action – Designing the City of Matter

This week, you’ll become an Atomic Architect, exploring how all matter in the universe is built from a limited number of elements. You’ll learn how the Periodic Table organizes these elements by their properties — and then bring that knowledge to life in VR by designing your very own futuristic city built entirely from metals, nonmetals, and noble gases.

Your city will tell the story of how everything — from glowing lights to living forests — is made of elements and compounds working together.

🤝 What to Expect This Week:

  • Learn how elements are grouped on the Periodic Table by their similar properties

  • Discover how atoms combine to form compounds that make up all living and nonliving things

  • Explore how scientists classify metals, nonmetals, and noble gases

  • Build and label a 3D Elemental City in VR that represents how matter is constructed

🎯 Spotlight Project:

🌆 The Elemental City– Architects of Matter

  • Build your Elemental City in Optima VR

  • Design three city zones:
    🏙️ Metal District – strong, shiny, and conductive
    🌿 Nonmetal Forest – gases and brittle solids that support life
    🌈 Noble Gas Sky Towers – glowing, floating lights of inert gases

  • Add at least three labeled compounds, such as:
    💧 Water (H₂O) 🧂 Salt (NaCl) 🌬 Carbon Dioxide (CO₂) 🌿 Glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) 🪨 Calcium Carbonate (CaCO₃)

  • Use light, color, and creativity to show each element family’s unique properties

  • Record a 1–3 minute VR walkthrough video explaining your city and its science

🧭 By the End of the Week, You’ll Be Able To:

  • Identify how elements combine to form compounds

  • Explain how the Periodic Table groups elements by similar properties

  • Use VR design to model how all matter is made of elements

  • Communicate science understanding through your Elemental City build

📌 Remember:

  • Use your Periodic Table & Elements Quick Reference Guide for help with element families and symbols

  • Label compounds clearly and include what elements make them up

  • Speak clearly during your video walkthrough

  • Need help or extra VR time? Join an Afterschool Session in Optima VR

  • Check Canvas for rubrics, examples, and updates

🌟 Mission Status:
Every atom tells a story of creation.
This week, build the universe — one element at a time.

– Ms. Orlando 🦈

pages.title: Week 3 Overview
pages.html:
⚗️ Classifying Matter– Unlocking the Properties of Substances

This week, you’ll become an AI Science Journalist investigating how scientists uncover the hidden identities of matter. You’ll research, compare, and report on the physical properties that make each substance unique — from metals that shine and conduct electricity to powders that dissolve in water.

You’ll also complete your Science Fair Mini-Experiments – Checkpoint 2 and take the Elements & Physical Properties Quiz to test your mastery of the week’s concepts.

🤝 What to Expect This Week:
• Learn how scientists classify and compare substances based on physical properties
• Explore measurable traits like density, solubility, conductivity, magnetism, and melting point
• Complete your Elements & Physical Properties Quiz
• Write and design your own front-page science article for The Matter Times
• Upload your Science Fair Mini-Experiments – Checkpoint 2 materials photo

🎯 Spotlight Projects:

📰 The AI Journalist – Reporting on the Science of Substances
Step into your role as a science correspondent for The Matter Times.
Write your feature article titled “The Secret Identity of Substances — How Scientists Classify Matter.”

Include:
• Headline & byline (By: [Your Name], Science Correspondent)
• Science Spotlight comparing two substances
• At least one AI-generated image on a Canva newspaper template describing the property being tested

💡 Choose two different substances to compare (examples: copper vs. aluminum, salt vs. sugar, metal vs. plastic).
Ask your AI assistant questions like:

“How can you tell copper and aluminum apart?”
“Why do metals conduct electricity while nonmetals don’t?”
“What tools measure density or melting point?”

🏛 Elements & Physical Properties Quiz
10 questions (multiple-choice and true/false)
Remember to use your quick reference guides and focus on identifying and classifying substances by measurable traits.

🔎 Science Fair Mini-Experiments – Checkpoint 2
Upload a clear photo of all your experiment materials for your chosen investigation.
Earn 5 points for clarity and completeness.

Stay on track for your Week 7 Science Fair video presentation!

Experiment Options:
🧂 Dissolving Race | 🌈 Skittles Spread | 🥤 Fizz Factory | 🧊 Ice Cube Melting Race | 🧲 Magnetic Mix | 🌱 Leaf Breathing | 🍎 Apple Browning

🧭 By the End of the Week, You’ll Be Able To:
• Classify and compare substances using measurable physical properties
• Explain how scientists test for conductivity, solubility, density, and magnetism
• Describe why physical properties are independent of sample size
• Communicate scientific findings through journalism and design
• Stay on track with your Science Fair project progress

📌 Remember:
• Use key vocabulary: density, conductivity, solubility, magnetism, melting point
• Label your visuals clearly and check for scientific accuracy
• Need to keep working? Join Optima VR after school

🌟 Mission Status:
Every substance has a story — your job is to reveal its identity.
Report the science. Compare the data. Write the truth behind the matter.

– Ms. Orlando 🦈

pages.title: Week 4 Overview
pages.html:
💡 Think Like a Scientist– The Method Behind Discovery

This week, you’ll step into the role of a true investigator — learning to think, question, and reason like a scientist. From real-world field notes to creative VR builds, you’ll explore how every discovery begins with curiosity, grows through experimentation, and ends in understanding.

You’ll practice using the scientific method in two different ways:
First, as a Field Scientist, you’ll head outdoors to make observations, record inferences, and form a hypothesis. Then, as a Science Trainer in VR, you’ll design Pokémon-style cards that bring each step of the scientific method to life — from asking questions to drawing conclusions.

🤝 What to Expect This Week:
• Learn and apply the six steps of the Scientific Method
• Practice observation, inference, and hypothesis skills in your field notebook
• Design creative Pokémon-style science cards in VR
• Record a 1–3 minute walkthrough video explaining each step in your own words
• Use Optima VR after school to finish your VR project or record your video

🎯 Spotlight Projects:

✏️ Field Scientist Challenge – Observation, Inference & Hypothesis

Become a real-world scientist and use your surroundings as your laboratory.

Write detailed observations of what you see, hear, or notice, make inferences about what those clues mean, and create a testable hypothesis in your own words.

Include:
• At least 3 observations (factual statements)
• At least 2 inferences (logical explanations)
• 1 hypothesis (If… then… statement)
• Clear photo of your completed notebook page uploaded to Canvas

💡 take a clear picture of your observations → inference → hypothesis in your notebook for submission. I have to be able to read your writing.

🎮 The Science Trainer Challenge – Mastering the Method

Join the Optima Science League and design six Pokémon-style cards, one for each step of the scientific method. Each card represents a different “Science Power” — from curiosity to discovery!

Your mission:
• Build your cards in Optima VR
• Label each card with the step name and a creative “move title”
• Write short 1–2 sentence descriptions in your own words
• Add color, energy effects, and creative designs to show each step’s “power”
• Record a 1–3 minute VR walkthrough explaining the six steps

📸 Don’t forget to take a snapshot of your model before logging out so you can finish later!

🧠 Examples to Inspire:
• Ask a Question – Curiosity Power (the spark of discovery)
• Research – Knowledge Boost (collecting clues before testing)
• Hypothesis – Prediction Attack (your best scientific guess)
• Experiment – Experiment Strike (testing your ideas)
• Analyze Results – Data Defense (looking for patterns)
• Conclusion – Discovery Evolution (sharing what you learned)

Each card should feel unique — like a collectible that captures the power of science itself.

🧭 By the End of the Week, You’ll Be Able To:
• Identify and explain the six steps of the scientific method
• Differentiate between observation, inference, and hypothesis
• Apply scientific thinking in both notebook and VR environments
• Communicate your understanding clearly and creatively
• Connect curiosity to discovery through evidence and explanation

📌 Remember:
• Use key vocabulary: observation, inference, hypothesis, experiment, data, conclusion
• Keep your explanations short and in your own words
• Take a snapshot of your model before leaving Optima VR
• Submit both projects to Canvas before Sunday night

🌟 Mission Status:
Every discovery begins with a question — your job is to follow the clues.
Observe the world. Build your cards. Explain your science.
Think like a scientist, and let curiosity lead the way.

– Ms. Orlando 🦈

💡 The Chemistry of Everyday Things – From Substances to Solutions

This week, you’ll step into the role of a Science Food Critic at The Chemical Café, where every menu item represents a different type of matter. From fizzy acids to sweet solutions, you’ll explore how chemistry hides in everyday foods and drinks.

Your challenge: order a full meal, stay under budget, and classify each item scientifically. You’ll practice identifying elements, compounds, mixtures, solutions, acids, bases, and salts — all while exploring our virtual café in Optima VR!

You’ll also continue your Science Fair Mini-Experiment, collecting data and uploading a photo of your trials for Checkpoint 3.

🤝 What to Expect This Week:
• Enter The Chemical Café VR experience in Optima VR
• Choose one drink, one appetizer, one main course, and one dessert under $20
• Classify each menu item using properties of matter
• Calculate your total and explain your reasoning on your whiteboard
• Take a clear VR snapshot or screenshot of your completed “meal”
• Upload your image and reasoning to Canvas
• Complete Science Fair Checkpoint 3 by uploading your data table and experiment photo

📘 Check Your Knowledge: Weekly Quiz!
At the end of the week, you’ll complete a 10-question quiz covering both:
• The six steps of the Scientific Method
• The chemistry of everyday items — including acids, bases, salts, and mixtures

Use your Quick Reference Guides to review before you begin. This short quiz is designed to help you see how well you understand the key ideas from the past two weeks.

🎯 Spotlight Projects:

☕ The Chemical Café – Matter Classification Challenge
Step inside our virtual café and explore the chemistry of food! Each menu item represents a scientific concept — from elements and mixtures to acids and bases.

Your mission:
• Order four items (drink, appetizer, main course, dessert)
• Identify each item’s type of matter
• Explain whether it can be separated physically or chemically
• Add up your total and confirm you stayed under budget
• Upload your VR or screenshot image showing your full meal and written classifications

💡 Remember: you can re-enter the café after hours in Optima VR if you need to finish the assignment from class or if you were absent.

🔎 Science Fair Mini-Experiments – Checkpoint 3
This week is all about data! Show your progress by uploading a photo of your experiment trials and data table.

Include:
• Clearly labeled data table
• Evidence of at least one full experiment trial
• Photo showing both your setup and results

📸 Upload one clear image to Canvas for Checkpoint 3.


🧪 Experiment Options:
• Dissolving Race (Salt vs. Sugar)
• Skittles Spread (Diffusion & Particle Motion)
• Fizz Factory (Baking Soda & Vinegar)
• Ice Cube Melting Race (Different Liquids)
• Magnetic Mix (Separating Mixtures)
• Leaf Breathing (Photosynthesis Bubbles)
• Apple Browning (Respiration & Enzymes)

🧭 By the End of the Week, You’ll Be Able To:
• Distinguish between pure substances and mixtures
• Identify and classify acids, bases, and salts
• Explain whether materials can be separated physically or chemically
• Present experimental data clearly using tables and photos
• Apply chemistry concepts to real-world examples

📌 Remember:
• Use Optima VR to complete or revisit the VR Café
• Include your total cost and classifications on your whiteboard
• Upload your Chemical Café image and Checkpoint 3 photo by Sunday night

🌟 Mission Status:

Science is everywhere — even in your lunch!
Explore the café, analyze what’s on your plate, and think like a chemist.
Every bite tells a story of matter in motion.

– Ms. Orlando 🦈

pages.title: Week 6 Overview
pages.html:
🌎 The Molecular Makeover Challenge – Conservation of Mass in Action
This week, we’re diving into the invisible world of atoms and molecules as we explore what truly happens during physical and chemical changes. You’ll build two accurate Bohr-model atoms using everyday household items, combine them into a molecule, and then rearrange the same pieces to model how atoms transform — without ever creating or destroying matter.

You’ll also continue preparing for your Science Fair Mini-Experiment by writing your video script and outline, giving you a strong foundation for your final presentation which is due next week.

By the end of the week, you’ll see exactly why scientists say: Matter can change… but it never disappears.

🤝 What to Expect This Week:

• Build two Bohr-model atoms using safe items from home
• Combine your atoms into a molecule using the exact same pieces
• Rearrange your molecule into a new structure to show mass is conserved
• Take two clear photos for your Atom Architect submission
• Complete Science Fair Mini-Experiment Checkpoint 4
• Write your video script or outline for your Science Fair presentation
• Use AI tools to help you create a strong, clear script based on the Video Checklist

🎯 Spotlight Projects:

⚛️ The Atom Architect Challenge – Building Atoms from the Inside Out
Choose two elements from Rows 1 or 2 of the periodic table and build each atom using household objects to represent protons, neutrons, and electrons. Use your Bohr diagram notes and pictures from class to set up the correct number of particles and electron shells.

Once both atoms are built, combine them into a molecule without adding or removing any pieces — then rearrange them into a different structure to model how atoms reorganize during chemical changes.

📸 Upload two photos to Canvas:
• Photo #1 — Both atoms built separately
• Photo #2 — Your molecule after bonding

✍️ Write a 3–5 sentence explanation describing your materials, your chosen elements, and how your model demonstrates the Law of Conservation of Mass.

🔎 Science Fair Mini-Experiments – Checkpoint 4
It’s time to start preparing what you’ll say in your Science Fair presentation!
For this checkpoint, you’ll write a clear script, outline, or bullet-point plan covering what your video will include.

Use the Video Checklist to guide your writing, and check the document attached to make sure you’ve included everything required for your final video submission due in week 7.

🌟 You are encouraged to use AI (like ChatGPT) to help you write your script.
You may type in your experiment details and the Video Checklist questions, and let AI help you form complete, organized sentences for your final script — just make sure the answers are written in your own words and reflect what you actually did in your experiment.

Please make sure your image is clear and readable for your submission.

The list of science experiments:

🧂 Dissolving Race — Salt vs. Sugar
🌈 Skittles Spread — Diffusion & Particle Motion
🥤 Fizz Factory — Baking Soda & Vinegar
🧊 Ice Cube Melting Race — Different Liquids
🧲 Magnetic Mix — Separating Mixtures
🌱 Leaf Breathing — Photosynthesis Bubbles
🍎 Apple Browning — Respiration & Enzymes

🧭 By the End of the Week, You’ll Be Able To:

• Build accurate atomic models based on Bohr diagrams
• Demonstrate the Law of Conservation of Mass using real objects
• Explain how atoms rearrange during chemical changes
• Prepare and organize a clear script for a scientific presentation
• Use AI tools responsibly to help revise or clarify your writing
• Communicate your understanding through photos, notes, and evidence

📌 Remember:

• Use ONLY the same objects for your protons, neutrons, and electrons
• Do not add or remove pieces when building your molecule
• Take clear, bright photos showing your atoms and your bonded molecule
• Your Science Fair script can be typed or handwritten — just be neat and complete
• You may use AI to help organize your script as long as the ideas are your own
• Submit all assignments by Sunday night in Canvas

🌟 Mission Alert:
From atoms to molecules and from experiments to explanations, this week you’ll discover how matter rearranges but never disappears. Build carefully, observe closely, and present confidently — because the way you model matter this week brings the invisible world to life. ✨

– Ms. Orlando 🦈

pages.html:
🎥 Lights, Camera, Experiment!– Science Fair Spotlight

This week, you’ve reached the final stage of your Science Fair Mini-Experiment journey — and your mission is simple and focused: record and submit your Science Fair Final Video Presentation.

This is the only assignment you have this week.

You’ll use your completed script and experiment visuals to create a clear, confident, and creative video explaining your mini-experiment from start to finish.

🤝 What to Expect This Week:

• Record your final Science Fair video
• Use your script as your guide
• Choose your video style (poster-board presentation or digital video)
• Include visuals from your actual experiment
• Explain your question, variables, results, claim, and reasoning
• Upload your video to Canvas
• No additional assignments this week 🎉

🎯 Spotlight Project:

🔎🎥 Science Fair Mini-Experiments — Final Video Presentation

📜 Objective

Your goal is to clearly explain your mini-experiment from start to finish using a recorded video. Your video must follow the Video Checklist and show that you completed each part of your experiment.

💬 Essential Question

“How can I communicate my scientific question, results, and reasoning clearly to others?”

🧑‍🔬 Your Mission

Create a short, organized video using either:

• A poster-board presentation, or
• A fully digital video made with images, captions, and experiment clips

Your video must include:

• Your question
• Your hypothesis
• Your IV, DV, and controls
• How you tested your experiment
• Your results
• Your claim
• Your reasoning

Keep it clear, confident, and easy to follow.

🧭 By the End of the Week, You’ll Be Able To:

• Communicate your experiment clearly
• Present scientific information using visuals
• Explain your data, claim, and reasoning
• Create a polished science video
• Submit your final Science Fair presentation

📌 Remember:

• Everyone must submit a video
• You choose the style — poster or digital
• Use visuals from your real experiment
• Stick to your script
• Follow the Video Checklist
• Submit by Sunday night

🌟 Mission Alert:

Videos must be submitted on time!

  • Late submissions may not be included in the Science Fair Gallery
  • Missing videos will impact subsequent assignments
  • Those follow-up assignments will result in a 0 that cannot be made up
    • (Remember to Submit by Sunday night in Canvas)

This is your big finale! Share your experiment with clarity and creativity — because this week, the spotlight belongs to you. 🎥✨

– Ms. Orlando 🦈

❄️ Operation Snowday – The Snowman Matter Mission

This week in 8th Grade Science, we’re venturing into the snowy Optima VR world to discover how matter changes— using VR, creativity, and storytelling to bring physical and chemical changes to life.

You’ll build, decorate, imagine, analyze, write, and communicate like true chemists as we transform a winter VR world into a Matter Change Storytelling Lab.

Your snowman won’t just be cute—
it will be the star of a scientific adventure about how matter transforms.

By the end of the week, you’ll be able to clearly explain the difference between physical changes and chemical changes while strengthening your model-building, storytelling, and science communication skills.

🤝 What to Expect This Week:

• Build a complete Snowday Snowman in Optima VR
• Use regular snowball objects only — no physics snowballs, no premade snowmen
• Decorate your snowman with required features (eyes, nose, mouth, arms)
• Give your snowman a personality, name, and backstory
• Choose one physical change and one chemical change
• Underline each change in your story
• Write a 3-paragraph Matter Change Story (4–6 sentences each)
• Upload one screenshot of your snowman + your typed or handwritten story
• Use Optima VR after school if you need more time in VR

🎯 Spotlight Projects:

☃️ Do You Want to Build a Snowman: The Matter Change Story

You are the Storytelling Scientist on a Snowday Mission.

Your task:
Build and decorate your snowman using regular snowball objects, then write a creative 3-paragraph story where your snowman experiences one physical change and one chemical change, each clearly explained and underlined.

📸 Upload One Clear Photo Showing:

• A full front view of your snowman
• All decorations and required features
• Any personality elements you added
• A clean, readable screenshot

✍️ Your Story (3 paragraphs, 4–6 sentences each):

Your story must include:
• A creative, engaging title
• One underlined physical change
• One underlined chemical change
• Explanation of how each change affected the snowman
• Strong creativity, detail, and scientific accuracy

🏛 Physical Science Final

Your Physical Science Final (worth 50 points) covers the major chemistry and science skills from the 8th grade module.


Your exam will include:

• Physical vs chemical changes
• Evidence of chemical reactions
• Conservation of mass
• Pure substances vs mixtures
• Elements, compounds, and particle models
• Matter and energy
• Scientific method
• Variables in experiments
• Nature of Science skills (models, hypotheses, evidence)


This is your final opportunity to demonstrate mastery before Winter Break.

🧭 By the End of the Week, You’ll Be Able To:

• Distinguish physical changes from chemical changes
• Identify evidence of chemical reactions
• Explain how matter is conserved during changes
• Build and document a VR scientific model
• Communicate ideas through creative writing and scientific explanation
• Evaluate investigations using evidence and reasoning
• Show mastery of essential 8th grade physical science concepts

📌 Remember:

• Use regular snowball objects — NOT physics snowballs
• Story must have 3 full paragraphs
• Underline one physical and one chemical change
• Snowman screenshot must be clear and fully decorated
• Be creative! Your snowman should have personality
• Re-enter Optima VR after school if you missed class or didn’t finish
• Upload your screenshot AND your story in Canvas by Sunday night

🌟 Mission Alert:

This week, you’re stepping into Frostvale Valley to explore how matter changes in the most magical, snowy way possible. Build boldly, write creatively, label clearly— and support your fellow scholars along the way.

Great scientists don’t just observe matter…
they explain it, transform it, and bring it to life. ❄️✨

– Ms. Orlando 🦈

🌆 The Elemental City– Architects of Matter

📜 Standards:
SC.8.P.8.5 – Recognize that there are a finite number of elements and that their atoms combine in many ways to make up everything we encounter.

SC.8.P.8.6 – Recognize that elements are grouped in the periodic table according to similarities in their properties.

🎯 Objective:
Design a futuristic VR city made entirely from elements and compounds to show how everything in the universe is built from the same building blocks of matter.

🌌 Mission Briefing:

Welcome, Architect.

You’ve been selected by the International Council of Atomic Architects to design a city unlike any other — The Elemental City, a living, glowing world built from the very atoms that make up reality itself.

Your city will rise across three unique zones, each powered by a family of elements from the Periodic Table. Metals will form your skyscrapers, nonmetals will breathe life into your forests, and noble gases will light up the skyline.

Your task is not just to build — but to prove that everything, from mountains to machines to living cells, is made from a finite set of elements that combine in infinite ways.

Design wisely. Let your city tell the story of how matter itself is made.

📝 Steps:

1️⃣ Plan Your City

Your Elemental City must include three distinct zones that represent the major element families:

  • 🏙️ Metal –
    Shiny, strong, and conductive. These elements build towers, bridges, and power systems.
    Examples: Iron (Fe), Copper (Cu), Aluminum (Al), Gold (Au).

  • 🌿 Nonmetal –
    The elements of life — found in the air, water, and all living things. Think parks or Forrests.
    Examples: Carbon (C), Oxygen (O), Nitrogen (N), Phosphorus (P), Sulfur (S).

  • 🌈 Noble Gas –
    Glowing, floating structures powered by inert gases that never react. Ballons, sky towers or neon decorations would be perfect for this part of the city.
    Examples: Helium (He), Neon (Ne), Argon (Ar), Krypton (Kr).

Pro tip: Sketch your zones before building so you know where everything belongs.

2️⃣ Design in VR

We will have class time to work on this assignment... If you do not finish building, make sure to take a snapshot of your model to load in and continue building your Element city for homework.

  • Enter Optima VR to finish your build and record your video once your city is complete

Build and label your city using creativity and scientific accuracy:

  • Create detailed structures for each of the three zones.

  • Add at least three labeled compounds that show how elements combine.

💡 Examples of Compounds You Can Include:

  • 💧 Water Fountain (H₂O) – hydrogen + oxygen, found in every living thing

  • 🧂 Salt Road (NaCl) – sodium + chlorine, found in oceans and food

  • 🌬 Carbon Dioxide Garden (CO₂) – carbon + oxygen, used by plants for photosynthesis

  • 🌿 Glucose Tree (C₆H₁₂O₆) – carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen; plant sugar that stores energy

  • 🪨 Calcium Carbonate Tower (CaCO₃) – forms shells, chalk, and limestone

  • 🔋 Rust Sculpture (Fe₂O₃) – iron + oxygen, formed when metal reacts with air

  • ☁️ Ammonia Cloud (NH₃) – nitrogen + hydrogen, found in fertilizers

  • 🔥 Methane Lamp (CH₄) – carbon + hydrogen, fuel gas used for energy

Each label should include:

  • Compound name

  • Element symbols

(Use sticky notes, letters in Optima VR, or a white board to label"

3️⃣ Record Your Walkthrough

🎥 Create a 1–3 minute VR video where you guide me through your Elemental City.

Show:

  • All three districts (Metals, Nonmetals, Noble Gases)

  • At least three labeled compounds — say their names and what they’re made of

  • How each zone represents its element family

Speak clearly and move slowly so your city’s science can shine!

🧱 Element Accuracy 10 Zones and compounds are scientifically accurate and correctly labeled.
🎨 VR Design & Creativity 10 City is detailed, organized, and visually represents science concepts.

📰 The Element Journalist – Reporting on the Science of Substances

Article Headline: “The Secret Identity of Substances — How Scientists Classify Matter”

📜 Standard

SC.8.P.8.4 – Classify and compare substances on the basis of characteristic physical properties that can be demonstrated or measured (for example: density, conductivity, solubility, magnetism, melting/boiling points), and know that these properties are independent of the amount of the sample.

🎯 Objective

Step into the role of an AI Science Journalist for The Matter Times!
You’ll research, write, and design a front-page science article that explains how scientists classify and compare substances based on their physical properties — using AI tools like ChatGPT or Gemini and Canva to create your layout.

🧠 Mission Briefing

Welcome, Journalist!

You’ve been assigned to write a feature story for The Matter Times, a global science publication uncovering the hidden identities of everyday materials.

Your article, titled “The Secret Identity of Substances — How Scientists Classify Matter,” will reveal how scientists use measurable, testable physical properties to tell substances apart — from metals that conduct electricity to powders that dissolve in water.

You’ll combine AI-powered research with your own creative writing and design skills to produce a newspaper-style front page that looks ready for print!

🧱 Substance Selection

Choose two substances to research and compare.
Your article should highlight at least two physical properties for each and explain how scientists can tell them apart.

Examples:

  • ⚙️ Metals: Copper, Aluminum, Iron, Nickel, Gold, Silver

  • 🌿 Nonmetals: Oxygen, Sulfur, Carbon, Phosphorus, Water

  • 🧂 Everyday Substances: Salt, Sugar, Soap, Ice, Plastic, Wood, Chalk

  • 💡 Special Substances: Magnetite, Graphite, Vinegar, Oil, Air

💡 Pro Tip: Pick substances with clearly different properties so your comparisons stand out!

📝 Steps to Complete

1️⃣ Research with AI

Use ChatGPT or Gemini to interview your “AI Lab Assistant.”
Ask questions that help you compare your two substances.
Examples include:

  • What properties help scientists tell copper and aluminum apart?

  • How do scientists test conductivity or magnetism?

  • Why doesn’t density change when you have more of a substance?

  • How do solubility and boiling point help identify materials?

Take notes and record at least two physical properties for each substance.

2️⃣ Write Your Article

Your front-page article must include:

  • 📰 A headline and byline (By: [Your Name], Science Correspondent)

  • ✍️ An intro paragraph that hooks the reader

  • 🔬 A Science Spotlight section comparing your two substances

  • 🧠 A conclusion explaining why physical properties don’t change with sample size

3️⃣ Design Your Front Page in Canva

  2. Search for “newspaper article template”

  3. Choose your favorite layout and replace the sample text with your own article

  4. Attach your AI-generated image directly into your design

📸 Your finished Canva design should include both your writing and your visuals — like a real science newspaper front page!

assignments.title: Science Notebook Entry: Field Scientist Challenge
assignments.html:
✏️ Science Notebook Entry: Field Scientist Challenge

📜 Standard

SC.8.N.1.1 – Define a problem from the eighth grade curriculum using appropriate reference materials to support scientific understanding, plan and carry out scientific investigations of various types, and communicate results.

Description:

In this assignment, you will become a field scientist — an explorer who studies the world through careful observation and evidence-based reasoning. Just like real scientists in nature, your job is to look closely at the world around you, notice small details, and use your observations to form logical explanations.

You’ll practice the first three steps of the scientific method — observation → inference → hypothesis. This means you’ll describe exactly what you see, explain what you think it means, and then make a scientific prediction that connects your evidence to your ideas.

You’ll be working outdoors or in your immediate environment, using your curiosity and senses to guide your investigation. The goal is not to “guess” what something is — but to think like a scientist, backing every statement with clear, descriptive observations. By the end, you’ll understand how scientists move from noticing patterns to forming testable hypotheses about the world.

🧭 Step 1: Title Page

Get out your science notebook and flip to a new page.

Title the page: Field Scientist Challenge

🔎 Step 2: Observe

Go outside or look closely around your environment. Take a few minutes to slow down and really notice the details that most people overlook. Scientists make careful, detailed observations using all of their senses — sight, sound, touch, and even smell — to gather facts about the world around them.

Look for patterns, textures, movements, and colors. Notice how light hits certain surfaces, how objects are arranged, or how animals or plants behave in their surroundings. Pay attention to both living and nonliving things — rocks, soil, leaves, insects, water, shadows, or even sounds in the distance.

Write down only what you can directly observe, not what you think it means. Observations should be factual and descriptive, not explanations or guesses.

Example: “I see a smooth, shiny surface with small ridges.”
Example: “I hear a faint buzzing sound coming from the flowers.”
Example: “The sky is bright with scattered white clouds.”

List at least three detailed observations in your notebook, but challenge yourself to go beyond three if you can! The more you notice, the stronger your scientific reasoning will be in the next step.

💡 Step 3: Infer

Now it’s time to think about what your observations might mean. Scientists use inferences to connect what they observe to what they already know. Inferences are educated explanations — they use evidence to make sense of what’s happening.

Review each of your observations and ask yourself questions like:

  • Why might this be happening?

  • What could have caused this pattern or behavior?

  • What do I already know that helps me explain this?

Your inferences should be logical and supported by your observations — not wild guesses or assumptions.

Example: “It looks like it could be metal because it reflects light.”
Example: “The buzzing sound might be from a bee collecting nectar.”

Write at least two inferences in your notebook that explain what you think might be going on based on the evidence you observed.

🧪 Step 4: Hypothesize

A hypothesis is your next step — a testable prediction based on your inferences and observations. It’s how scientists turn curiosity into questions that can be tested or explored further.

Look back at your notes and choose one of your inferences to build a hypothesis from.
Use one of these formats:

  • “I think the object is ___ because ___.”

  • “If the object is ___, then it will ___.”

Make sure your hypothesis connects directly to your observations and could be tested in a real experiment or future investigation.

Example: “I think the object is a microscope lens because it’s round, reflective, and used in science labs.”
Example: “If the buzzing sound is from a bee, then I should see it moving near flowers collecting pollen.”

Write your final hypothesis neatly in your notebook and underline it so it stands out.

📸 Step 5: Submit Your Work

  1. Take a clear photo of your notebook page.

  2. Upload the image to Canvas under this assignment.

📊 Rubric

Category Points Description
🔍 Observations 3 Three or more clear, evidence-based observations written in notebook.
💡 Inferences 3 Two or more logical inferences supported by observations.
🧪 Hypothesis 3 One complete and reasonable hypothesis using correct format.
📤 Submission 1 CLEAR photo uploaded to Canvas.

💯 This assignment is worth 10 points.

Remember: Great scientists see the world with curiosity first — not just looking, but truly observing. 🌎👀

🎮 The Science Trainer Challenge – Mastering the Method

📜 Standards:

SC.8.N.1.2 – Design and conduct a study using repeated trials and replication.

SC.8.N.1.3 – Use phrases such as “results support” or “fail to support” in science, understanding that science does not offer conclusive “proof” of a knowledge claim.

SC.8.N.2.1 – Distinguish between scientific and pseudoscientific ideas.

SC.8.N.2.2 – Discuss what characterizes science and its methods.

SC.8.N.1.6 – Understand that scientific investigations involve the collection of relevant empirical evidence, the use of logical reasoning, and the application of imagination in devising hypotheses, predictions, explanations, and models to make sense of the collected evidence.

🎯 Objective:
Design a VR deck of Pokémon-style science cards that illustrate each step of the scientific method, then record a short walkthrough video explaining the process in your own words.

🌌 Mission Briefing:

Welcome, Science Trainer. ⚡

You’ve been chosen by the Optima Science League to master the greatest scientific technique in history — the Scientific Method.

Your mission: create six Pokémon-style cards in VR that represent each step of the method, from asking questions to drawing conclusions. Each card will showcase the power of curiosity, experimentation, and discovery through creative visuals and scientific accuracy.

Once your deck is complete, you’ll record a VR walkthrough explaining the steps of the scientific method in your own words — showing that you understand not just what scientists do, but how they think.

Remember: every great discovery starts with a question. Your job is to show how those questions evolve into answers. 🌟

📝 Steps:

1️⃣ Design Your Science Cards

Create six Pokémon-style cards, one for each step of the scientific method:

  • Ask a Question – Curiosity Power

  • Research – Knowledge Boost

  • Form a Hypothesis – Prediction Attack

  • Test with an Experiment – Experiment Strike

  • Analyze Results – Data Defense

  • Draw Conclusions – Discovery Evolution

Each card must include:

  • Step name and creative “move” title

  • A 1–2 sentence description written in your own words explaining that step

  • A creative Pokémon or science character

  • Energy color, icon, or design theme that fits the “power”

💡 Pro Tip: Sketch your ideas or plan in your science notebook before building your cards in VR.

🎨 Pokémon Card Inspiration Table

Use these examples to spark your creativity—but make each card your own!

Step Example Pokémon Card Concept “Move” or Power Description Idea
Ask a Question 🔍 Inquisitoron – a curious scientist Pokémon holding a magnifying glass Curiosity Power Uses observation energy to spot mysteries no one else sees.
Research 📚 Datadillo – a small creature rolling through libraries and data clouds Knowledge Boost Gains power from collecting facts, notes, and background info.
Form a Hypothesis 💡 Predictara – a glowing orb Pokémon that senses patterns Prediction Attack Creates an “If...then...” beam that forecasts results.
Test with an Experiment ⚗️ Testachu – a lightning-fueled lab Pokémon that activates reactions Experiment Strike Tests its predictions using precision tools and controlled trials.
Analyze Results 📊 Graphadon – a wise data dragon that studies charts and outcomes Data Defense Reflects false results and protects valid data from error attacks.
Draw Conclusions 🌟 Evolucent – a radiant final-evolution Pokémon that gains clarity Discovery Evolution Uses evidence to transform understanding into discovery.

🌈 Be creative!
You can base your characters on animals, lab tools, mythical creatures, or even abstract ideas (like Photonix the light analyzer or HypothiSaurus the reasoning dino).

As long as your cards clearly show what happens in each step of the scientific method, your imagination can run wild!

2️⃣ Build in VR

Enter Optima VR to build your Science Trainer Arena.

In your VR space:

  • Display your six cards in order from Step 1 → Step 6.

  • Use props, lights, and effects to make each step feel unique.

  • Add floating labels or arrows to show the progression.

  • Use a whiteboard, sticky notes or floating text to include your short explanations. (Just make sure that I can read your writing while you are explaining your steps.)

📸 Important:
Take a snapshot of your model before logging out so you can reload your project and continue working after school if you don’t finish during class.

Use Optima VR after school to record your video and finish working on your cards.

*** I will also link the cards at the bottom of the assignment so you can add them into Optima VR... (Visit Tech Help if you do not know how to add images into Optima VR) ***

3️⃣ Record Your Walkthrough

🎥 Create a 1–3 minute VR video showing your full build.

In your video, explain:

  • Each of the six steps of the scientific method in your own words

  • How each card represents that step

  • How the scientific method connects from start to finish

Speak clearly and move slowly so your design and science ideas shine!

assignments.html:
⚛️ The Atom Architect Challenge– Matter That Never Disappears

📜 Standard:

SC.8.P.9.1 – Mass is conserved during physical and chemical changes.

🎯 Objective:

Use everyday household items to build two accurate atom models (based on the Bohr diagrams we made in class). Then use the exact same pieces to create a molecule and rearrange it into a new molecule, proving that no matter is created or destroyed.

🧰 Materials

Use ANY safe small items from your home.
Choose three different item types to represent:

  • Protons

  • Neutrons

  • Electrons

Examples you may use:
buttons, pasta, Legos, beads, cereal, pom-poms, coins, paperclips, Q-tips, pipe cleaners, cotton balls, stickers, rocks, tiny toys

Material Rules:

  • All protons = same item type

  • All neutrons = same item type

  • All electrons = same item type

  • Use ONLY these items for the whole project

  • Do NOT add or remove pieces later

🧪 Instructions

1️⃣ Choose Two Elements (Rows 1 or 2 Only)

Pick TWO elements from this list:

Row 1:

  • Hydrogen (H)

  • Helium (He)

Row 2:

  • Lithium (Li)

  • Beryllium (Be)

  • Boron (B)

  • Carbon (C)

  • Nitrogen (N)

  • Oxygen (O)

  • Fluorine (F)

  • Neon (Ne)

For EACH element, look up and write down:

  • Number of protons

  • Number of neutrons

  • Number of electrons

  • Number of electron shells

💡 You may use your Bohr diagram notes and pictures from class to help you.

2️⃣ Build Atom #1

A. Build the nucleus

  1. Count out the correct number of protons.

  2. Count out the correct number of neutrons.

  3. Group them tightly together to form one nucleus.

B. Build the electron shells

  • Shell 1: up to 2 electrons

  • Shell 2: up to 8 electrons

Use things like:

  • Circles drawn on paper

  • Pipe cleaners shaped into rings

  • String or yarn taped into circles

  • A paper plate with rings drawn on it

Place electrons on the correct shells based on your element.

C. Label your atom

Write a label that includes:

  • Element name

  • Element symbol

  • Atomic number

  • “Atom 1”

D. Check your work

Make sure:

  • Protons = atomic number

  • Neutrons match what you wrote down

  • Electrons are in the correct shells

  • It matches your Bohr diagram notes from class

3️⃣ Build Atom #2

Repeat all of the steps from Atom #1 for your second element:

  • Build the nucleus

  • Build the shells

  • Label it “Atom 2”

  • Check it with your notes

📸 Take Photo #1:
Both atoms fully built, labeled, and shown separately before bonding.

4️⃣ Bond Your Atoms Into a Molecule

Use all of the pieces from both atoms:

  • Combine them into one molecule

  • Do NOT add any new pieces

  • Do NOT remove any pieces

  • Do NOT change which items represent which particles

  • All pieces should still be visible

Ways you can show bonding:

  • Move nuclei closer together

  • Connect atoms with a toothpick, string, or paper strip

  • Place shared electrons between atoms

  • Build one clear combined structure

📸 Take Photo #2:
Your completed molecule after bonding.

5️⃣ Rearrange Into a New Molecule

Take the molecule apart and rebuild it into a different arrangement using the exact same pieces.

Rules:

  • Use every piece you started with

  • Do not add or remove anything

  • Make the new arrangement clearly different in shape/structure

This shows how atoms can rearrange in a chemical change while the total amount of matter stays the same.

(No extra photo is needed for this step.)

6️⃣ Write Your Explanation (3–5 sentences)

In your own words, explain:

  1. What objects you used for protons, neutrons, and electrons

  2. Which two elements you chose

  3. How your model shows that no matter was created or destroyed

  4. How your model demonstrates the Law of Conservation of Mass

*** Use complete sentences.

📝 Assignment Submission

Submit the following:

📸 1. Two Required Photos

  • Photo #1: Both separate atoms before bonding

  • Photo #2: The molecule after bonding

✍️ 2. Written Explanation (3–5 sentences)

Explain your materials, your elements, and how your model shows that mass is conserved.

📊 Rubric (20 points)

Category Points Description
🧬 Explanation & Understanding 10 Clearly explains materials, chosen elements, and how the model shows the Law of Conservation of Mass.
⚛️ Model Accuracy & Photos 7 Atoms and molecule are accurate, labeled, neat, and both required photos are submitted. No pieces added or removed.
🎨 Creativity & Effort 3 Creative material choices, neat construction, and strong effort shown.

💯 Total: 20 points

🏠 The Great Gingerbread House Temperature Challenge

📜 Standard
SC.8.P.9.3 – Investigate and describe how temperature influences chemical changes.

🎯 Objective
Decorate a gingerbread house in VR, model how extreme heat causes chemical changes, and explain how extreme cold would prevent those chemical changes from happening.

You will submit two VR images and one written paragraph to demonstrate how temperature influences chemical reactions.

🧠 Mission Briefing

Welcome, Gingerbread Chemist!

Today you will step into the role of a temperature investigator, combining VR creativity with real chemical science. Your mission is to explore how temperature influences chemical changes by observing what happens when ingredients like sugar, chocolate, candy, and gingerbread are exposed to extreme heat — and then explaining how those same reactions would be prevented by extreme cold.

Inside Optima VR, you will decorate your own gingerbread house in our Winter Kitchen simulation. Every candy piece you place and every 3D-pen detail you add will help you illustrate how heat transforms ingredients chemically, forming brand-new substances.

After decorating your house, you will simulate a brush fire event, demonstrating how high temperatures cause:

  • Burning

  • Caramelization

  • Charring

  • Decomposition

  • Smoke and soot production

These reactions let you SEE how heat speeds up molecular motion and triggers irreversible chemical changes.

Then, you will switch roles and become a Cold Zone Analyst, explaining how an Ice Age-level freeze would prevent these reactions. You will describe how cold:

  • Slows molecular motion

  • Prevents chemical reactions from starting

  • Stops new substances from forming

  • Halts browning, burning, and decomposition

Your job is to compare what DOES happen in heat to what CANNOT happen in cold, showing how temperature controls chemical change.

By the end of this mission, you will have:

  • Decorated a scientific model

  • Simulated a real chemical phenomenon

  • Identified evidence of chemical change

  • Used chemistry vocabulary correctly

  • Written a scientific analysis

  • Produced visual documentation in VR

You’re not just decorating — you’re modeling real chemistry.

🍬 Gingerbread House Instructions

Use candy pieces, your 3D pen, and other 3D-pen–drawn candy or gingerbread house elements to decorate your creation.

Be creative — detailed decorations make the chemical changes easier to show.

2️⃣ Include decorations that realistically undergo chemical reactions
Choose items that burn, caramelize, or decompose under heat, such as:

  • Sugar-based candy

  • Chocolate-inspired designs

  • Icing-like 3D-pen patterns

  • 3D-pen–drawn gumdrops, peppermints, candy canes, or chocolate bars

These will help you model clear chemical changes after the brush fire.

🔥 Brush Fire Scenario – Extreme Heat (Chemical Changes Only)

Simulate what would happen if a brush fire swept through your gingerbread village.

High temperatures cause chemical reactions that create new substances.

Examples of chemical changes caused by heat:

  • Gingerbread burns → ash, char, smoke

  • Sugar decorations caramelize or burn

  • 3D-pen “icing” scorches and decomposes

  • Candy decorations melt and chemically break down

  • Smoke, soot, and burnt odors form

You must modify your gingerbread house in VR to show these heat-driven chemical changes.

3️⃣ Cold-Prevention Paragraph (4–6 sentences)

Write this in the Canvas text box or comments.

Explain why extreme cold prevents chemical changes from happening and how this relates to your gingerbread house.

Remember:
Cold temperatures slow molecules down, which means chemical reactions cannot start, and no new substances can form.

Use this reminder to write a clear, complete explanation.

assignments.title: Science Fair Showcase: Scholar Review Panel
assignments.html:
🎥 Science Fair Showcase– Scholar Review Panel

📜 Standards:

SC.8.N.1.1 – Define a problem from the eighth-grade curriculum, use appropriate reference materials to support scientific understanding, plan and carry out scientific investigations of various types (such as observations, experiments, or modeling), identify variables, collect and organize data, interpret data in charts/tables/graphics, analyze information, and defend conclusions.

SC.8.N.1.2 – Design and conduct a scientific investigation using repeated trials and replication.

SC.8.N.1.3 – Distinguish between experimental (test) groups and control groups in scientific investigations.

SC.8.N.1.4 – Explain how hypotheses are valuable even if they turn out to be incorrect.

SC.8.N.1.5 – Analyze the methods used by scientists to test hypotheses and explain why scientific investigations must be replicable.

SC.8.N.1.6 – Understand that scientific investigations involve the collection of evidence, reviewing explanations, and comparing those explanations to the evidence collected.

SC.8.N.1.7 – Recognize the importance of communication in science by identifying various methods used to report and explain experimental results.

SC.8.N.1.8 – Use appropriate tools and techniques to gather, analyze, and interpret data.

🎯 Objective:
Watch at least 3 Science Fair Project videos and evaluate the strength of each investigation using the Nature of Science standards — focusing on variables, evidence, data, explanations, replicability, and the clarity of each scholar’s communication.

🌌 Mission Briefing:
Welcome, Scholar Reviewer.

You have entered the Optima Science Fair Showcase — a lineup of investigations created by your fellow scholars. Your mission is to watch at least five videos and provide thoughtful, evidence-based, and encouraging feedback.

You may comment on:

  • The strength of the experiment

  • How the scholar communicated

  • The clarity of their video or visuals

  • Their use of variables or data

💛 Important:
Your feedback must be kind, supportive, and encouraging only.

Absolutely no negative, rude, or discouraging comments will be tolerated.

You are reviewing the work, not the person — and every scholar deserves respect.

We lift each other up in science. 🌟

🧰 Steps:

1️⃣ Watch at least 3 Science Fair videos
Choose any projects from today’s showcase.

2️⃣ Take brief notes while watching
Record observations about:

  • Variables and data

  • Conclusions and evidence

  • Presentation and communication

  • Visuals and clarity

  • Replicability

3️⃣ Write your reflection in your science notebook
Use complete sentences and label your answers clearly.

📝 Assignment Submission

Submit the following:

📸 1. A photo of your written reflection in your science notebook
Your handwriting must be clear, and the full page must be visible.

✍️ 2. Your Reflection (2–3 complete sentences for each question):

  1. Which Science Fair video was your favorite and why?
    You may comment on the experiment, the science, the video quality, or how clearly the scholar communicated.

  2. Which project helped you learn something new?
    Explain what the scholar tested and what you learned from their experiment or their presentation.

  3. Did you watch at least 3 videos?
    (Yes or No)
    Name or briefly describe one of them.

💛 Encouragement Reminder:
Your answers must be respectful, positive, and encouraging.
Only kind, uplifting feedback will be accepted.

📊 Rubric (10 points):

Category Points Description
🧠 Reflection Responses 6 Answers are clear, thoughtful, encouraging, and reference specific videos or observations.
🎥 Participation 2 Student confirms watching at least 5 videos and describes at least two.
✔️ Notebook Photo 2 Student uploads a clear photo of their handwritten reflection page.

💯 Total: 10 points
